area-basic-figures.why: Every area formula comes from the rectangle. A parallelogram is a rectangle with a triangle moved from one end to the other. A triangle is half a parallelogram. A trapezium is the average of its two parallel sides times the height. Knowing why makes the formulas hard to forget.
traps: The height must be *perpendicular* to the base, not the slanted side.
The trapezium formula averages the two *parallel* sides; the slanted sides are not involved.

composite-area.why: Awkward shapes are usually simple shapes added together or taken apart. Split an L into two rectangles, or subtract a corner from a bigger one. Choosing the easiest split is most of the skill.
traps: Keep exact values such as ~\pi~ until the last step. Rounding early shifts the final answer.
When subtracting, check the removed piece really lies inside the whole shape.

perimeter-problems.why: Perimeter is the distance round the outside, and many practical problems — fencing, edging, trim — are perimeter problems with a twist: a side missing, a wall instead of a fence, a curved part. Read exactly which edges count.
traps: A semicircle's perimeter includes its straight diameter edge as well as the curve.
Fencing against a wall needs fewer metres than the full perimeter. Read which sides are needed.
